topics.name: The Elements of Art
facts: The Elements of Art are all nouns.
Line is a mark or stroke made with a material.
Tone is the application of light, medium and dark shades, often used to create a 3D or realistic effect.
Colour refers to the tints or shades we perceive from light reflecting off objects or surfaces.
Shape is a flat outline without tone, and appears to be 2D.
Form is a 3D object, or an image which appears to be 3D.
Texture refers to the qualities of a surface and how it feels, e.g. rough or smooth.
Shape is 2D while Form is 3D — tone is used to turn a shape into a form.

topics.name: Shading Techniques (turning shapes into forms)
facts: Six shading techniques are used to turn shapes into forms: Hatching, Cross Hatching, Blending, Rendering, Squiggly, and Contour Hatching.
Hatching uses parallel lines to create tone.
Cross Hatching uses overlapping sets of parallel lines crossing each other to build up darker tone.
Blending smooths shading so there are no visible lines between tones.
Rendering creates smooth, gradual tone, often using soft pencil work.
Squiggly shading uses small scribbled or squiggly marks to build tone.
Contour Hatching uses curved lines that follow the form of the object to suggest its 3D shape.
These techniques apply tone to a 2D shape to make it appear 3D (a form).

retrieval_questions.q: Name the six shading techniques on the revision sheet.
retrieval_questions.a: Hatching, Cross Hatching, Blending, Rendering, Squiggly, Contour Hatching.

topics.name: Colour and Blending
facts: Colours can be grouped as Complimentary, Cool/Warm, or Harmonious.
Harmonious colours are colours that sit next to each other on the colour wheel and blend together best.
Complimentary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel.
Cool colours include blues, greens and purples; warm colours include reds, oranges and yellows.
Tone can be created in colour by adding lighter or darker shades of the same hue.
Blending two colours together involves gradually transitioning from one colour into another with no hard edge.
Observational drawing means copying what you see accurately from a reference image.
The cell image studied is used as a reference for observational drawing and colour blending practice.
